title: Data structures, ADTs and algorithm analysis
subtitle: Choose how to store data, and know how the cost of working with it grows. This chapter builds the vocabulary — structure, ADT, algorithm, Big-O, recurrence, amortised cost — that every later chapter uses.

why.title: Why structure matters
why.body:
Every program does two things: it stores data and it computes on it. How the data is arranged decides how hard the computing is. Imagine a phone book. Arranged alphabetically, you find “Sharma” by opening in the middle and halving the search, about ten steps for a thousand names. Arranged in the order people were added, you would have to read every entry. The information is identical; only the structure differs, and the difference between ten steps and a thousand is the whole subject of this course.

A data structure is a way of organising data in memory so that the operations you need are cheap. An array gives instant access by index but costly insertion in the middle; a linked list inserts cheaply at a known place but finds slowly; a hash table finds almost instantly but keeps no order; a balanced tree does everything in logarithmic time and keeps order. No structure wins every operation — choosing one is choosing which operations you want to be fast.

Separate from how data is stored is what you can do with it. An abstract data type (ADT) is a specification: a set of values and the operations on them, with their meaning, but no mention of memory layout. A stack is an ADT — push, pop, peek, “last in, first out” — and it can be implemented on an array or on a linked list without any user of the stack noticing. That separation is the same one you met in operating systems (abstraction hides implementation) and in object-oriented programming (a class exposes an interface). Data structures are the implementations; ADTs are the contracts.

classes.title: Kinds of data structure
classes.body:
Structures are sorted in a few overlapping ways. By construction: primitive types (int, char, float, pointer) are built into the language; non-primitive structures are built from them. Non-primitive structures split into linear ones, where elements form a sequence and each (except the ends) has one predecessor and one successor — arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues — and non-linear ones, where an element may relate to many others — trees and graphs. By memory: static structures have a fixed size decided at compile time (a plain array); dynamic ones grow and shrink at run time (linked list, vector). By storage: contiguous (array: neighbours in memory) or linked (nodes anywhere, joined by pointers).

The rest of this course walks the map in order: stack and recursion (Chapter 2), queues and lists (3–4), trees (5), graphs (6), then the two big algorithmic topics that use these structures — sorting (7) and searching and hashing (8). Each chapter builds the structure, analyses its operations with the notation of this chapter, and then shows an algorithm that depends on it.

algo.title: What an algorithm is
algo.body:
An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined steps that solves a problem. Five properties are required. Input: zero or more values supplied from outside. Output: at least one result. Definiteness: each step is precise and unambiguous (“add 1 to x”, not “improve x”). Finiteness: for every input it terminates after a finite number of steps. Effectiveness: each step can be carried out in finite time with pencil and paper. A recipe that says “stir until nice” fails definiteness; a loop with a condition that never becomes false fails finiteness.

An algorithm is not a program. The same algorithm — binary search — can be written in C++, Python or pseudocode; the program is one way of expressing it. We therefore describe algorithms in pseudocode (structured English with loops and conditions) or as flowcharts and then analyse the idea, not the language.

design.title: Algorithm design techniques
design.body:
Algorithms are rarely invented from nothing; they come from a small toolbox of strategies. Brute force tries every possibility — correct and easy, often hopeless for large inputs. Divide and conquer splits the problem into smaller copies of itself, solves each (usually recursively) and combines the answers — merge sort, quick sort, binary search. Greedy algorithms build a solution by always taking the best-looking local choice and never reconsidering — Huffman coding, Kruskal’s and Prim’s spanning trees, Dijkstra’s shortest path; they are fast but correct only when the problem has the right structure. Dynamic programming solves overlapping subproblems once and stores the answers (Fibonacci, shortest paths between all pairs, knapsack). Backtracking builds a solution step by step and undoes the last step when it hits a dead end (N-queens, maze solving); branch and bound adds pruning by a bound on the best possible result. Randomised algorithms use random choices (random pivot in quick sort) to avoid bad worst cases.

Recognising which strategy a problem fits is half the skill of an algorithm designer. As a rule of thumb: if the problem splits into independent halves, think divide and conquer; if subproblems repeat, think dynamic programming; if a local best choice can be proved safe, think greedy; if nothing else works and the input is small, brute force with pruning.

analysis.title: Measuring an algorithm: counting, not timing
analysis.body:
How do we compare two algorithms? Timing them is unreliable — it depends on the machine, the compiler, the language and what else is running. Instead we count how many basic operations the algorithm performs as a function of the input size n, in an idealised RAM model: every elementary operation (assignment, comparison, arithmetic, array access) takes one unit of time. The result is a function T(n), and what matters is how it grows. If doubling n doubles T, the algorithm scales linearly; if doubling n quadruples T, it scales quadratically.

The cards below count real operations. Bubble sort on 5 1 4 2 8 makes 9 comparisons and 4 swaps; merge sort makes 8 comparisons. On five numbers the difference is small. The point of analysis is to predict what happens at five million, where one grows as n² and the other as n log n.

best.title: Best, worst and average case
best.body: The cost of an algorithm often depends on which input of size n it receives. Linear search for a value in an array stops at the first match, so it needs 1 comparison if the target is first (best case), n if it is last or absent (worst case), and on average about half. The worst case is the one analysts quote by default, because it is a guarantee: no input can make the algorithm slower. The best case is rarely informative (every sorting algorithm is fast on already-sorted data in some way). The average case needs an assumption about the distribution of inputs, usually “all equally likely”, and is harder to compute but often more representative — quick sort is O(n²) in the worst case yet O(n log n) on average, which is why it is used everywhere.
best.steps: Linear search in an array of n distinct elements. The target is equally likely to be at any of the n positions. Position i needs i comparisons. Average comparisons = (1 + 2 + … + n) / n. Simplify. For n = 8 that is 4.5 comparisons on average, against 8 in the worst case — both are Θ(n).

big.title: Asymptotic notation: O, Ω, Θ
big.body:
We now make “grows like” precise. We care about behaviour for large n and ignore constant factors (different machines change them) and lower-order terms (they are swamped). Big-O gives an upper bound: f(n) = O(g(n)) if there are constants c > 0 and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. Big-Omega gives a lower bound: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) if f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for large n. Big-Theta is both: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) when f is squeezed between two constant multiples of g — the tight bound. Little-o and little-ω say “strictly smaller” and “strictly larger”.

A few rules make this mechanical. Drop constants: 5n = O(n). Keep the dominant term: n² + n log n + 100 = O(n²). Sum: O(f) + O(g) = O(max(f, g)). Product: O(f)·O(g) = O(f·g). A sequence of two code blocks costs the larger; nested blocks multiply. Limit test: if lim f(n)/g(n) is finite, f = O(g); if it is a positive constant, f = Θ(g); if it is 0, f = o(g). Beware the common confusion: Big-O is an upper bound, not “the worst case” — you can say the best case is O(n) too. And O(n²) is a true statement about linear search (it is also O(n)), just a loose one; the tight claim is Θ(n).

The order of the standard functions, slowest-growing first: 1 < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!. The table shows how fast they separate; the second shows what that means in wall-clock time at a billion operations a second.
big.steps: Show 3n² + 5n + 20 = O(n²): choose c and n₀ with 3n² + 5n + 20 ≤ c·n² for n ≥ n₀. For n ≥ 1: 5n ≤ 5n² and 20 ≤ 20n², so the sum is at most 28n². Now show 3n² + 5n + 20 = Ω(n²): trivially 3n² + 5n + 20 ≥ 3n² for all n ≥ 0, so c = 3 works. Both bounds hold, hence the function is Θ(n²). Disproof by contradiction: is n³ = O(n²)? It would need n³ ≤ c·n², i.e. n ≤ c for all large n — impossible for any constant c.

loops.title: Analysing loops and code
loops.body: To analyse a piece of code, count how often its innermost statement runs. The rules are simple. A statement is O(1). A sequence costs the sum, which is the larger term. A single loop to n with an O(1) body is O(n). Nested loops multiply: two loops to n give O(n²). A loop whose counter doubles or halves (i *= 2, n /= 2) runs about log₂ n times, because that is how many doublings it takes to reach n. A loop whose inner bound depends on the outer variable needs a sum: for i … for j = i+1 … runs 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2 times — still O(n²), because the sum of the first n integers is quadratic. Run each program: the DSA Lab counts the iterations.
loops.steps: Analyse: for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) for (j = 1; j <= i; j++) c++;. The inner loop runs i times for each i. Total iterations is the sum 1 + 2 + … + n. Which is Θ(n²); for n = 4 the count is 10.

recur.title: Recurrences: analysing recursive algorithms
recur.body: A recursive algorithm’s cost is described by a recurrence: T(n) is expressed in terms of T on smaller inputs. Binary search does one comparison and recurses on half: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Merge sort sorts two halves and merges in linear time: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. A naive Fibonacci calls itself on n − 1 and n − 2: T(n) = T(n − 1) + T(n − 2) + 1, which grows exponentially. Three tools solve them. Substitution guesses the answer and proves it by induction. The recursion tree draws the calls level by level and sums the work per level. The master theorem handles the divide-and-conquer form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n): compare f(n) with n^{log_b a}. If f is smaller, T = Θ(n^{log_b a}); if equal, T = Θ(n^{log_b a} log n); if larger (and regular), T = Θ(f).
recur.steps: Binary search: each call does constant work and halves the interval. Unroll the recurrence k times. The recursion ends when the interval has size 1, i.e. when n/2^k = 1, so k = log₂ n. Substitute k: T(n) = T(1) + log₂ n. Merge sort via the recursion tree: level 0 does n work; level 1 has two subproblems of n/2 each, again n in total; every one of the log₂ n levels does n work. Master theorem check: a = 2, b = 2, so n^{log_2 2} = n, which equals f(n) = n; the middle case gives Θ(n log n). Solve T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n using the master theorem. Compare f(n) = n with n^{log₂ 4} = n². f is polynomially smaller, so the leaves dominate.

amort.title: Amortised analysis: the cost of many operations together
amort.body:
Worst-case analysis can be pessimistic when an expensive operation is rare. Consider a dynamic array (C++ vector): adding an element is O(1) when there is room, but when the array is full it must allocate a bigger one and copy every element, costing O(n). Is each push_back then O(n)? Not on average. If the capacity doubles each time it fills, the expensive copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, … and the total copying over n insertions is 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n/2 < n. So n insertions cost O(n) in total — O(1) amortised per insertion. Amortised cost is the average over the worst-case sequence, not a probabilistic average: it is a guarantee about any sequence of operations.

Run the program: 100 insertions into an array that starts with capacity 1 and doubles. The final capacity is 128 and the total number of elements copied is 127 — barely more than one copy per insertion.
amort.steps: Insert n elements into an array that doubles its capacity when full. Copy cost at the doubling that happens when the size is 2^i is 2^i elements. A geometric sum: the last term is more than the sum of all earlier ones. Add the n ordinary insertions (1 unit each). Total work is less than 3n, so the amortised cost per insertion is at most 3 — a constant.

space.title: Space complexity and the time–space trade-off
space.body: Time is not the only resource. Space complexity counts the extra memory an algorithm needs beyond its input, again as a function of n. Merge sort needs O(n) extra space for the merge buffer; heap sort sorts in place with O(1) extra; quick sort needs O(log n) of stack on average (and O(n) in the worst case). A recursive algorithm also uses space for its call stack — a recursion n levels deep costs O(n) stack even if it allocates nothing else. Often you can trade one resource for the other: a lookup table or memoisation spends memory to avoid recomputation; compressing data spends time to save memory. Knowing the trade-off lets you choose by constraint: on a phone with little RAM, in-place; in a server with spare memory and strict latency, precompute.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• A data structure arranges data so needed operations are cheap; an ADT states the operations without the implementation. No structure wins every operation.
  • An algorithm is finite, definite and effective; common strategies are brute force, divide and conquer, greedy, dynamic programming and backtracking.
  • Cost is counted in operations as a function of n: best, worst and average cases can differ; the worst case is a guarantee.
  • O is an upper bound, Ω a lower bound, Θ a tight bound; keep the dominant term, drop constants. Order: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < 2ⁿ < n!.
  • Loops: sequence adds, nesting multiplies, halving/doubling gives log n, dependent inner bounds give sums such as n(n−1)/2.
  • Recurrences (substitution, recursion tree, master theorem) analyse recursion: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 is O(log n); T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n is O(n log n).
  • Amortised analysis averages over a sequence: doubling arrays give O(1) amortised insertion. Space complexity and recursion depth matter too.
